blogs.title: Standing in the Shadow of Administrative Discretion: Why AFL’s Claim Failed
blogs.description: An in‑depth look at the D.C. Circuit’s standing analysis in America First Legal Foundation v. Jamieson Greer, focusing on the Court’s application of the Lujan test, the “procedural injury” doctrine, and the limits of redressability when a plaintiff seeks to compel an agency’s internal investigation. The post will explore how this decision reinforces the high bar for informational standing and the implications for future FOIA‑related suits against oversight bodies like the OSC.

blogs.title: Statutory Interpretation of 5 U.S.C. § 1216: Does the OSC Have a Mandatory FOIA‑Investigation Duty?
blogs.description: This article dissects the competing readings of § 1216(a)(3) and § 1216(c) that underpinned the district court’s and appellate courts’ decisions. It examines precedent on statutory “shall” language, the interplay with FOIA’s own enforcement provision (§ 552(a)(4)(F)(i)), and the broader question of whether Congress intended to bind the OSC to investigate alleged FOIA violations regardless of the trigger provisions.

blogs.title: The Role of Discretionary Enforcement in the Civil Service Reform Act: Lessons from the OSC’s Refusal to Investigate
blogs.description: A policy‑focused piece analyzing how the Court’s deference to the OSC’s discretion under §§ 1214 and 1215 reflects longstanding “Heckler‑Chaney” principles. The post will discuss the balance between agency accountability and executive flexibility, the potential chilling effect on FOIA enforcement, and suggestions for legislative reform to clarify the OSC’s investigative obligations.

blogs.title: FOIA, the OSC, and the Future of Judicial Recusal Transparency: What This Case Means for Access to Government Email
blogs.description: While the case turned on standing, the underlying factual dispute concerns DOJ’s policy of not searching employee emails without consent. This blog will explore the broader transparency implications for judicial recusal investigations, compare DOJ’s approach to other agencies, and consider how courts might address similar FOIA policy challenges absent standing hurdles.
